headline: Wastewater connectivity at Vala de Ançã — agricultural reach marks it as an AMR surveillance candidate
mechanism: Treated and untreated wastewater is the dominant route by which antibiotic resistance genes enter urban surface water. OneAquaHealth found clinically relevant pathogens and high resistance gene loads in urban stream biofilms across its pilot cities.
evidence: sewage odour reported, indicating recent foul input
citations: Recast Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive, Article 17 (AMR surveillance)
OneAquaHealth Key Indicators factsheets (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20345207)
actionCitizen: No individual action is warranted on this finding. Reporting the location of outfall pipes and any discharge from them helps build the map this assessment depends on.
actionMunicipal: Article 17 of the recast Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive requires AMR monitoring for agglomerations of 100,000 population equivalents and above. Sites like this one are where that sampling belongs.
actionHealth: Candidate site for environmental AMR surveillance. Resistance genes require qPCR or metagenomics — this is a pressure proxy derived from discharge connectivity, never a measurement.

headline: Invertebrate community at Vala de Ançã — agricultural reach is dominated by pollution-tolerant taxa
mechanism: Sensitive groups — stonefly, mayfly, cased caddisfly — disappear first under organic pollution and low oxygen, leaving worms, bloodworm and hoglouse. Because the community reflects conditions over months rather than the moment of sampling, this indicates sustained pressure, not a single event.
evidence: ASPT 4.18, against a site reference of 6.0
citations: UKTAG (2009), Recommendations on Surface Water Status Classification
OneAquaHealth Key Indicators factsheets (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20345207)
actionCitizen: Repeat the kick-sample survey next season. Community change is slow, so a consistent series from the same reach is worth far more than any individual survey.
actionMunicipal: Chronic pressure rather than an acute incident. Investigate persistent inputs and physical habitat in the Ançã catchment; restoring riparian cover is usually the highest-return intervention available.
actionHealth: Not a direct human exposure signal, but a degraded community is a reliable marker of sustained wastewater influence, which is the same pathway that carries resistance genes and enteric pathogens.

headline: Oxygen depletion at Vala de Ançã — agricultural reach beyond what temperature explains
mechanism: Oxygen is being consumed faster than it is replenished. Organic loading drives microbial respiration that strips oxygen from the water column; below roughly 4 mg/L, sensitive invertebrates and fish cannot persist.
citations: UKTAG (2009), Recommendations on Surface Water Status Classification
actionCitizen: Photograph and report any dead or distressed fish, sewage smell, or greyish water. These observations time-stamp an event that intermittent official sampling will otherwise miss.
actionMunicipal: Trace organic inputs upstream in the Ançã catchment: sewer misconnections, farm or industrial discharges, and blocked outfalls. Prioritise if the depletion persists across consecutive visits.
actionHealth: Low oxygen is not itself a direct human health hazard, but it reliably co-occurs with organic and faecal contamination. Treat as an indicator that warrants microbiological sampling rather than as an exposure risk on its own.

headline: Nutrient enrichment at Vala de Ançã — agricultural reach
mechanism: Elevated nitrogen and phosphorus drive excessive algal and plant growth. The subsequent decay consumes oxygen, and in warm, slow water the same enrichment is the precondition for cyanobacterial blooms.
citations: UKTAG (2009), Recommendations on Surface Water Status Classification
OneAquaHealth Key Indicators factsheets (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20345207)
actionCitizen: Keep recording nutrient test-kit readings. Nutrient concentrations swing widely between visits, so the value is in the series rather than in any single result.
actionMunicipal: Identify nutrient sources in the Ançã catchment — wastewater discharge, agricultural runoff, misconnected drainage. Riparian buffer restoration reduces diffuse input and improves habitat at the same time.
actionHealth: Indirect concern. Enrichment raises the probability of a cyanobacterial bloom, which is a direct hazard where the water has public or animal contact.

headline: Stream health at Vala de Ançã — agricultural reach has declined 17 points over 30 days
mechanism: A sustained downward trend that is steepening over the last week. Progressive deterioration of this shape usually reflects an accumulating input rather than a discrete incident.
citations: UKTAG (2009), Recommendations on Surface Water Status Classification
actionCitizen: Keep sampling on the same schedule. A consistent series is what makes a trend visible at all — gaps are what hide it.
actionMunicipal: Review what has changed in the Ançã catchment over the last month: construction, land use change, new connections, or altered discharge patterns.
actionHealth: No immediate exposure concern. Worth tracking, because sustained ecological decline in an urban stream generally accompanies rising wastewater influence.

headline: Conditions consistent with a combined sewer overflow at Ribeira de Coselhas — Loreto
mechanism: Rainfall exceeded combined sewer capacity, allowing untreated wastewater to reach the watercourse alongside stormwater.
evidence: 16 mm of rain in the preceding 48 hours
0 dry day(s) immediately before the storm
catchment is served by a combined sewer
visible discharge reported in 100% of visits
citations: EU Bathing Water Directive 2006/7/EC, Annex I (CELEX:32006L0007)
OneAquaHealth Key Indicators factsheets (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20345207)
actionCitizen: Avoid contact with the water for at least 48 hours after heavy rain. Report any strong sewage smell or visible discharge with a photograph.
actionMunicipal: Inspect sewer overflow structures and outfalls in the Coselhas catchment within 48 hours. Check for blockages, misconnections and consent breaches, and confirm whether a spill was logged.
actionHealth: Treat as elevated faecal exposure risk. Bathing Water Directive inland limits are 500 cfu/100 ml E. coli and 200 cfu/100 ml intestinal enterococci at the 95th percentile — Neer cannot measure these, so confirmatory sampling is required before any classification.

headline: Mosquito breeding conditions present at Ribeira de Coselhas — culverted reach
mechanism: Culex pipiens — the principal West Nile virus vector in Europe — breeds in stagnant, organically rich water and in the artificial containers that accumulate as litter. Transmission has been demonstrated from 18 °C upward, so temperate sites are not exempt.
evidence: water temperature 28.7 °C, within the transmission envelope
organic enrichment indicated by low dissolved oxygen
citations: ECDC West Nile virus factsheet; Culex thermal competence 14–34.3 °C
OneAquaHealth Key Indicators factsheets (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20345207)
actionCitizen: Remove containers that hold standing water — tyres, buckets, cans. Report pooling and blocked channels, which is where breeding concentrates.
actionMunicipal: Clear litter and debris, and restore flow through pooled or blocked sections. Notify the vector surveillance programme if one operates in this municipality.
actionHealth: Consider for vector surveillance siting. Neer does not survey mosquitoes — OneAquaHealth DipteraCAST addresses that directly, and this finding is a habitat indicator rather than a vector count.
